episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Wednesday, March 18, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education.
-
Today, writing faculty pass a resolution affirming their right to refuse A.I. in the classroom, while the White House releases a framework that includes workforce development as a core principle.
-
In Insights and Trends today, the White House has released its A.I. policy framework for Congress, outlining six guiding principles for lawmakers developing A.I. governance policies.

According to WTAE, among these principles is, quote, educating Americans and developing an A.I.-ready workforce, end quote. The framework aims to preempt state-level regulations while ensuring, quote, all Americans benefit from this technological revolution, end quote.

Workforce development sits alongside priorities like protecting children, safeguarding communities, and ensuring American A.I. dominance. The framework does not specify what A.I.-ready means in practice. This leaves room for interpretation about whether it refers to technical skills like coding and prompt engineering, or broader competencies like critical thinking about A.I.-generated content.
-
Turning to Ethical A.I., the Conference on College Composition and Communication passed a resolution affirming the rights of students and faculty to decline generative A.I. use in writing classrooms.

According to Inside Higher Ed, the resolution was overwhelmingly approved at CCCC's annual convention in Cleveland. Jennifer Sano-Franchini of West Virginia University stated this is an academic freedom issue. The resolution cites unsubstantiated productivity claims, data privacy concerns, and threats to critical thinking. Over 1,000 education professionals globally signed an open letter opposing mandatory A.I. adoption in education.
-
In Case Studies, Austin Community College District announced a human-centered A.I. initiative supported by an $875,000 three-year grant from the Trellis Foundation.

According to ACC Newsroom, the initiative includes A.I.-powered student support to identify barriers early and connect students to advising, tutoring, financial aid, and mental health resources, launching in April 2026. Nationally, nearly 40 percent of community college students fail to earn a credential within six years. ACC will also create an A.I.-focused workforce pathway including an Electrician Certification program for digital infrastructure careers. Chancellor Russell Lowery-Hart emphasized doing this in a way that privileges humanity.
-
Also in Insights and Trends, the U.S. Department of Labor released a voluntary A.I. literacy framework outlining five content areas and seven delivery principles to guide workforce training nationwide.

According to the Department of Labor, the framework prioritizes hands-on experiential learning and human skills like judgment, creativity, and communication over abstract A.I. theory. Secretary of Labor Lori Chavez-DeRemer stated the framework will help accelerate effective A.I. skill development. The initiative follows guidance promoting WIOA funding for A.I. skills training.
-
In another Case Study, a survey of 29 local agencies around Chattanooga, Tennessee found that 20 have no A.I. policies in place.

According to the Chattanooga Times Free Press, experts warn this creates security and privacy risks for government operations. The few agencies with policies emphasize A.I. as a tool to help humans, not replace them, with explicit guidelines for appropriate use.
-
That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

topStory.headline: White House A.I. Framework Includes Workforce Development as Core Principle
topStory.summary:
The White House released its A.I. policy framework for Congress, outlining six guiding principles for lawmakers developing A.I. governance policies, according to WTAE. Among these principles is "educating Americans and developing an A.I.-ready workforce." The framework aims to preempt state-level regulations while ensuring "all Americans benefit from this technological revolution."

Workforce development sits alongside priorities like protecting children, safeguarding communities, and ensuring American A.I. dominance. The framework comes as President Trump signed an executive order in December blocking states from crafting their own A.I. regulations, arguing that inconsistent rules would hurt sector growth.

The framework does not specify what "A.I.-ready" means in practice, leaving room for interpretation about whether it refers to technical skills like coding and prompt engineering, or broader competencies like critical thinking about A.I.-generated content and understanding algorithmic bias.
